# MIMIC × Ghost

> Your first users shouldn't be your testers. MIMIC is a multi-agent synthetic usability testing tool: six AI personas with different, code-enforced behaviours go through your site in parallel, each in its own isolated browser, and MIMIC shows where they got stuck, with evidence for every finding.

The web app needs JavaScript and a backend that may take 30–60 s to wake up on free hosting. This file and the GitHub README describe the project in plain text.

## What it does

1. Configure: a target URL, a goal ("buy a policy") and optional success criteria, plus an authorization confirmation.
2. Cohort: six personas, each with explicit traits, an action budget and a frustration threshold.
   - Impatient: small budget, low patience, never waits, quits early when blocked (qwen3.8-27b on Groq)
   - Low digital literacy: only sees controls with visible text labels; error messages frustrate it more (Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite)
   - Power user: shortest path, no browsing; its path length shows wasted steps (qwen3.8-27b)
   - Cautious: must check fees and terms before committing on payment, OTP or consent pages (gpt-oss-120b on Groq)
   - Explorer: opens secondary paths and backtracks without frustration (Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite)
   - Chaos: edge-case inputs (12345, Devanagari digits, emoji), double-clicks, going back mid-flow (gpt-oss-120b)
3. Swarm: six parallel Playwright browser contexts with no shared cookies or storage; every step streams live over server-sent events and a journey map draws each route.
4. Report: deterministic metrics (completion, abandonment, average and median actions, unique paths, backtracks) and findings split into Observed → Evidence → Interpretation → Suggested investigation. Model-written interpretations are labelled as AI-written.
5. Replay: step by step, what the persona saw, what it decided and why, what happened, how its state changed, and screenshots.

## Agentic loop

observe page (compact text: headings, messages, numbered element menu) → reason as persona (LLM picks ONE action from the menu as JSON; it cannot invent selectors) → persona policy (code-enforced behaviour) → act (Playwright) → update state (deterministic rules: frustration, progress, budget, journey memory) → continue | success | abandoned | failed | budget exhausted | blocked by verification.

Code owns state, the LLM owns choices. The model can't end its own journey by claiming "done": success is checked against the criteria. Findings come from 13 deterministic friction detectors over stored events; the LLM only rewrites interpretation text and cannot add findings or change evidence.

## Measured results

Tested against SurakshaSetu, a fictional health-insurance onboarding site we built with 13 documented usability defects (12 detectable from text and behaviour), so results are scored against ground truth.

Recorded demo run: 2 min 54 s with six personas in parallel; 2 reached the goal (Power, Cautious), 3 gave up (Impatient, Low literacy, Explorer), 1 ran out of actions (Chaos); 5 different routes; 11 findings, each linked to events and screenshots; 6 of 12 seeded defects found; 0 errors. Three of six personas gave up on the same mobile OTP page, which has two seeded defects (silent 3 s OTP, code shown only in small footer text). Across six scored runs during development, MIMIC found 42–83% of seeded defects.

## Architecture

Next.js UI (Vercel) → HTTPS + SSE → FastAPI on Modal: run orchestrator with 6 LangGraph persona loops; one Chromium with 6 isolated contexts; model router (Groq for decisions, Gemini for decisions, fallback, screenshot reading and report wording, with per-model token-bucket rate limiting); event bus to Supabase; analysis (metrics, 13 friction detectors, clustering); tracing to LangSmith.

## Safety

Authorization checkbox on every run; private and loopback targets rejected (SSRF guard); navigation fenced to the target host; irreversible actions blocked except on our demo site; CAPTCHA and Cloudflare challenges end the persona with no bypass; rate limits on starting runs.
